paras: The whipping of Dave Stokes was an assault on a Black man by the town marshal of Soperton, Montgomery County, Georgia, around the turn of 1903. Marshal T. H. Blizzard whipped Stokes for taking a drunken man home without his consent, and a few nights later four Black men fired on the marshal in what the white press called an attempted murder. Three Black men were jailed afterward, while Stokes himself was hunted by officers.

Soperton was described as a new town on the line of the Macon, Dublin and Savannah road. Its marshal, T. H. Blizzard, objected that Stokes had carried a drunken man to his home and put him to bed "without the marshal's knowledge or consent."

For this Blizzard whipped Stokes, and Theo. Rogers either helped administer the whipping or was present when it was given. According to Rogers, Stokes's friends were "incensed" and swore vengeance on both men. A few nights later, a night or two before Jan. 6, four Black men fired on Blizzard in town; the marshal returned fire, and no one was hit.

The next morning Frank Stokes, Fab Stokes and Bob Brown were arrested and taken to jail at Mt. Vernon, while Dave Stokes remained at large with officers said to be close on his tracks. Brown's captors, Rogers, Charles Outlier and M. C. Dinkins, said he was the man who had tried to kill the marshal at Adrian months earlier and planned to claim a $75 reward. In September 1903 a Swainsboro dispatch reported that a Bob Brown, said to be the man who shot at the Soperton marshal, had shot a deputy sheriff's horse while resisting arrest and escaped into a swamp. No report of a trial of the arrested men, or of any charge against Blizzard or Rogers, was found.

The episode is known from a single Dublin dispatch in the Savannah Morning News on Jan. 7, 1903, headlined "Lively for a New Town" and based entirely on Rogers's account. The dispatch mentioned the whipping only as the prelude to what it called "the attempted murder" of the marshal, and it carried no word from Stokes or the arrested men. When the same paper returned to Brown in September under the headline "Fired on by a Negro," it described him as "very desperate" and did not mention the whipping. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The September item placed the shooting at the Soperton marshal "last year," which fits only if it occurred in the final days of 1902, while the January dispatch, the contemporaneous report, put it a night or two before Jan. 6.

accounts.label: Theo. Rogers via Dublin dispatch
accounts.gist: Blizzard whipped Stokes for taking a drunk man home without consent; Stokes's friends swore vengeance and four of them fired on the marshal; three were arrested.

accounts.label: Swainsboro dispatch
accounts.gist: Bob Brown, who shot at the Soperton marshal 'last year', fired on a deputy sheriff serving a warrant and escaped to the swamp.

framing.detail: Under the headline 'Lively for a New Town' the Savannah Morning News relayed Rogers's version, treating the whipping as an aside and the retaliatory shooting as 'the attempted murder'.
The September item, 'Fired on by a Negro', calls Brown 'very desperate' and mentions the Soperton shooting only as his record.

versions.value: A night or two before a Jan. 6, 1903 dispatch

conflicts.note: Both can fit if the shooting fell in the last days of 1902; A1 is the contemporaneous report and the better evidence for timing.

sources.note: Dublin, Ga., Jan. 6 dispatch on Theo. Rogers's account: Marshal Blizzard whipped Dave Stokes; four Black men later fired on the marshal; three arrested and jailed at Mt. Vernon.
quotes: Mr. Blizzard whipped a negro named Dave Stokes, who carried a drunken man to his home and put him to bed without the marshal's knowledge or consent.
Mr. Rogers assisted in whipping the negro, or was present when it was administered.
The friends of Stokes were incensed at the action of Messrs. Blizzard and Rogers, and swore vengeance.
